intro: A playing field is built for a game, but it is never only a game place. A team's employer runs it. A league writes its rules. A city or park district may own the ground. A flag flies over it, and an anthem plays before the first whistle. In this unit you will study what happens when athletes use that crowded space to protest, and when players argue about who gets paid and seen.

The first chapter follows protest on the field, from an Irish jumper on a flagpole in Athens in 1906 to a playoff game that never started in 2020. You will read the First Amendment, two Supreme Court cases about students, and one about a coach. The second chapter follows women's and men's professional sport as two industries, from a wartime baseball league in Rockford, Illinois, to equal-pay contracts signed in 2022.

By the end, you will be able to name the body that wrote a rule, the law that limits it, and the year it changed. You will be able to state a money gap in dollars and explain where the money comes from. And you will practice choosing one frame, such as labor, law or civic life, and using it clearly in an argument.
bigQuestion: When a playing field becomes a place to argue about rights, pay and recognition, whose rules decide what may happen there?

title: Field as Square

chapters.title: Protest on a Field
chapters.bigQuestion: When an athlete protests during a game, is the field a workplace, a public square, or a national stage, and who gets to decide?

story.title: A Quiet Stadium
story.kicker: A crowd stands for a song, and a few players on the sideline do something else.
paragraphs: A fall afternoon in a big American football stadium. The public address announcer asks the crowd to rise. Tens of thousands of people stand up. A singer walks to a microphone near midfield. Players line the sidelines with helmets in their hands. The first notes of "The Star-Spangled Banner" fill the air.

Most players stand with a hand over their heart. A few players on one sideline kneel on one knee instead. They do not shout. They do not leave. Cameras swing toward them at once. By the time the song ends, photos of the kneeling players are already moving across phones in every time zone.

The argument that follows is loud, but it is also old. People ask whose ground this is. The team owns the uniforms. The league writes a game operations manual. A city or park district may own the stadium itself. Fans paid for tickets. Each of those facts points to a different answer about what a player may do there.

Historians of sport have seen this scene before, in other forms. An Irish jumper climbed a flagpole in Athens in 1906. A champion boxer refused the military draft in 1967. Two sprinters raised gloved fists on a medal stand in 1968. Each time, a place built for a game became a place where a country argued with itself.
story.think: Who do you think has the strongest claim to decide what happens on a playing field during the anthem: the player, the team, the league, the stadium owner, or the crowd? Why?

lessons.title: A Flag on a Pole, 1906
lessons.mainIdea: At the 1906 Games in Athens, Irish athlete Peter O'Connor climbed a flagpole to wave an Irish flag, because he had been entered under Britain.
reading: In 1906 Athens held an extra Olympic-style event, now called the *Intercalated Games*. Intercalated means placed in between. The event fell between the 1904 and 1908 Olympics. The International Olympic Committee (IOC) does not count it as an official Olympics today. Still, athletes from many nations came, and crowds filled the rebuilt marble stadium, the Panathenaic Stadium.

Ireland was then part of the United Kingdom, ruled from London. Irish athletes were entered as part of the British team. Peter O'Connor, a jumper from Ireland, objected. He wanted to compete for Ireland. The officials listed him under Britain anyway. O'Connor held the world record in the long jump at the time, set in Dublin in 1901.

O'Connor placed second in the long jump in Athens. When the British flag went up for him, he climbed the flagpole. He waved a green flag with a gold harp and the words "Erin go Bragh," an Irish phrase often translated as "Ireland forever." A teammate, Con Leahy, helped guard the pole. O'Connor later won the triple jump.

The episode shows a pattern that returns again and again. Games sort athletes by *nation*. A flag rises for each winner. An athlete who disagrees with the flag has a stage the whole crowd can see. Ireland's own Olympic team first competed separately in 1924, two years after the Irish Free State was founded in 1922.

words.d: the 1906 multi-sport event in Athens held between regular Olympics; the IOC does not count it as official
a people and country that claims its own government, flag and team
the ceremony of lifting a winner's national flag during a medal presentation

look.title: Two Flags, One Jumper
look.text: Athens, 1906. Officials raise the British flag for the second-place long jumper. The jumper was born in Ireland and wants to compete for Ireland. He climbs the pole and waves a green flag with a harp. His teammate stands guard at the bottom.
look.prompt: What did the jumper's action say about who should decide which nation an athlete stands for?

check.q: Why did Peter O'Connor climb the flagpole in 1906?
choices: He was entered under Britain but wanted to represent Ireland.
He had lost the race and was angry at the judges.
He wanted to fix a broken rope on the pole.
He was protesting the Olympic amateur rule.
check.why: Ireland was under British rule, so O'Connor was listed under Britain. He waved an Irish flag to show he competed for Ireland.

check.q: What are the Intercalated Games?
choices: an extra event in Athens in 1906 that the IOC does not count as official
a Chicago contest during the 1893 fair
check.why: The 1906 Athens event fell between the 1904 and 1908 Olympics, and the IOC does not list it as an official Games.

check.q: When did Ireland first send its own separate Olympic team?
check.why: Ireland first competed separately in 1924, after the Irish Free State was founded in 1922.

lessons.title: A Champion Refuses the Draft
lessons.mainIdea: In 1967 heavyweight champion Muhammad Ali refused induction into the U.S. Army, lost his title and license to box, and won his case at the Supreme Court in 1971.
reading: Cassius Clay won Olympic gold in boxing at Rome in 1960. In 1964 he won the world heavyweight title. Soon after, he announced he had joined the Nation of Islam. He took the name *Muhammad Ali*. Many newspapers kept calling him Clay for years, which was itself a kind of argument about who he was.

The United States was fighting in Vietnam, and young men were called up by a *draft*. A draft is a law that orders people into military service. Ali asked to be exempt as a minister of his faith and a conscientious objector, a person who refuses to fight for reasons of belief. On April 28, 1967, in Houston, he refused to step forward for induction.

Boxing was run by state commissions and sanctioning bodies, not one national league. Within days, they stripped his title and suspended his license. In June 1967 a federal jury convicted him of refusing the draft. He was sentenced to five years in prison but stayed free while he appealed. He did not box for more than three years, from age 25 to 28.

In 1971, in *Clay v. United States*, the U.S. Supreme Court overturned his conviction by a vote of 8 to 0. The justices found that the government had not given a proper reason for rejecting his claim. Ali's case showed that a sports license, a title and a prison sentence could all hang on one act of refusal made far from any ring.

words.d: a law that orders people into military service
a person who refuses to fight in war because of religious or moral belief
an organization that approves fights and awards titles in a sport like boxing
heavyweight boxing champion, born Cassius Clay, who refused the draft in 1967

look.title: Three Kinds of Power
look.text: In 1967 three separate powers acted on one boxer. A state athletic commission took away his license to fight. Boxing bodies took away his title. A federal court sentenced him to prison. Four years later, the U.S. Supreme Court overturned the conviction.
look.prompt: Which of these three powers belonged to the sport, and which belonged to the government? Explain the difference.

choices: to fight a title bout in Chicago
to sign a contract with a new promoter
check.why: Ali refused induction in Houston, claiming exemption as a minister and conscientious objector.

check.q: What happened in Clay v. United States in 1971?
choices: Ali was barred from boxing for life.
The Supreme Court overturned his conviction 8 to 0.
Ali won back his title in the ring that day.
check.why: The Supreme Court overturned Ali's draft conviction by a vote of 8 to 0.

check.q: Who took away Ali's license to box?
check.why: Boxing was run by state commissions and sanctioning bodies, which suspended his license and stripped his title.

lessons.title: Fists on a Medal Stand, 1968
lessons.mainIdea: At the 1968 Mexico City Olympics, Tommie Smith and John Carlos raised gloved fists during the U.S. anthem, and U.S. officials sent them home under IOC pressure.
reading: On October 16, 1968, the men's 200-meter final ran at the Mexico City Olympics. Tommie Smith of the United States won in a world record of 19.83 seconds. Peter Norman of Australia was second. John Carlos of the United States was third. Mexico City's high altitude helped many sprint times that year.

On the medal stand, Smith and Carlos stood in black socks without shoes, a sign of Black poverty. Each raised a fist in a black glove as "The Star-Spangled Banner" played. They bowed their heads. All three medalists wore badges of the *Olympic Project for Human Rights* (OPHR), a group that sociologist Harry Edwards helped found in 1967.

IOC president Avery Brundage, an American from Chicago, said politics did not belong at the Games. The IOC pressed the U.S. Olympic Committee to act. The U.S. committee suspended Smith and Carlos and sent them home from Mexico City. Both men received hate mail and threats in the following years. Brundage himself had led the U.S. Olympic Committee before he led the IOC from 1952 to 1972.

The photograph of the *podium* became one of the best-known images of the 1960s. Decades later, the view changed in some places. San José State University, where both sprinters had studied, unveiled a statue of the moment in 2005. The U.S. Olympic and Paralympic Hall of Fame inducted Smith and Carlos in 2019.

words.d: a group founded in 1967 to press sports bodies on racism; its badge was worn on the 1968 podium
the raised stand where medal winners receive their medals
to remove someone from a team or event for a period as a penalty

look.title: The 1968 Olympic 200-Meter Final
look.cite: Official Report of the Games of the XIX Olympiad, Mexico City, 1968
look.prompt: How many seconds separated the winner from the bronze medalist?

check.q: Who founded the Olympic Project for Human Rights with others in 1967?
check.why: Sociologist Harry Edwards helped found the OPHR in 1967.

check.q: What did the U.S. Olympic Committee do after the podium protest?
choices: It gave the sprinters a second medal.
It moved the medal ceremony to a new day.
It suspended Smith and Carlos and sent them home.
It pulled the whole U.S. team out of the Games.
check.why: Under IOC pressure, the U.S. committee suspended the two sprinters and sent them home.

check.q: What did Peter Norman wear on the podium?
choices: an Australian flag as a cape
check.why: All three medalists, including Norman, wore Olympic Project for Human Rights badges.

lessons.title: Comiskey Park, 1918
lessons.mainIdea: The Star-Spangled Banner was played at the 1918 World Series in Chicago during World War I and became the national anthem by law in 1931.
reading: Francis Scott Key wrote the words of "The Star-Spangled Banner" in September 1814. He watched British ships bombard Fort McHenry in Baltimore during the War of 1812. The poem was set to an older British tune. For the next hundred years it was one patriotic song among several. It was not yet the official *national anthem*.

In September 1918 the Chicago Cubs played the Boston Red Sox in the World Series. The Cubs used Comiskey Park, the larger home of the White Sox, for their home games. The United States had entered World War I the year before. Many players had been drafted, and the season had been cut short by a government order about war work.

During the seventh-inning stretch of Game 1, on September 5, a band played "The Star-Spangled Banner." Newspaper reports say the crowd stood and sang. Red Sox infielder Fred Thomas, who was on leave from the U.S. Navy, stood at attention and saluted. The song was played at later games in the Series too.

Congress made "The Star-Spangled Banner" the national anthem by law on March 3, 1931. During World War II, playing it before games became common in many ballparks and arenas. Over time it became a set part of the *pregame ritual*, the fixed steps that happen before play starts. That custom began as wartime patriotism, not as a rule written by any league.

words.d: a song adopted by a country as its official patriotic song
the fixed ceremonies that happen before a game begins, such as the anthem
the championship series of Major League Baseball, first played in 1903

look.title: A Song Finds a Ballpark
look.text: Chicago, September 5, 1918. The country is at war. The crowd at Comiskey Park is smaller than usual. In the middle of the seventh inning, a band starts a patriotic song. A ballplayer on leave from the Navy turns to the flag and salutes. The crowd joins in.
look.prompt: Why might a wartime crowd have wanted a patriotic song at a ballgame? What does that tell you about where the custom came from?

check.q: Where was the anthem played during the 1918 World Series game described in the lesson?
check.why: The Cubs played their 1918 Series home games at Comiskey Park, the larger White Sox ballpark.

check.q: When did The Star-Spangled Banner become the national anthem by law?
check.why: Congress adopted it as the national anthem on March 3, 1931.

check.q: What does pregame ritual mean?
choices: the fixed ceremonies that happen before play starts
a rule about how long a game lasts
the score at the start of a game
check.why: A pregame ritual is a set ceremony, like the anthem, that happens before a game begins.

lessons.title: Rules About Standing
lessons.mainIdea: Leagues and national federations have written rules about the anthem, and players such as Mahmoud Abdul-Rauf and Megan Rapinoe tested them.
reading: A league can write rules for its games in documents such as a *game operations manual*. These rules cover uniforms, time between periods, and ceremonies. For many years the NBA's rules said players, coaches and trainers should stand and line up in a dignified posture during the anthem. That rule came from the league, not from any law of the United States.

In March 1996, Denver Nuggets guard Mahmoud Abdul-Rauf stayed seated or stretched in the tunnel during the anthem. He said that as a Muslim he viewed the flag as a symbol of oppression. The NBA suspended him without pay. The suspension lasted one game. He then agreed to stand and pray silently during the song, with his head bowed.

In September 2016, soccer player Megan Rapinoe knelt during the anthem before a U.S. women's national team match. The *federation*, U.S. Soccer, is the national body that runs the team. In 2017 its board adopted a policy that players should stand during the anthem. In June 2020, U.S. Soccer voted to repeal that policy.

Each case shows that anthem rules are written by specific bodies at specific times. A league or federation can change its own rule by a vote. Players can push for a change through a union or in public. The rule belongs to the organization that wrote it, and that organization is also the one that can remove it.

words.d: a league document of rules for how games are run, including ceremonies
a national or world body that governs one sport and its teams
to cancel a rule or law officially

look.title: Two Rule Makers
look.text: Case one: a professional league suspends a player for one game for sitting during the anthem, and the player later agrees to stand and pray. Case two: a national soccer federation adopts a policy in 2017 that players stand, then repeals it in 2020.
look.prompt: In each case, who wrote the rule, and who had the power to change it?

check.q: Who suspended Mahmoud Abdul-Rauf in 1996?
check.why: The NBA suspended him for not standing, under its own rule about the anthem.

check.q: What did U.S. Soccer do in June 2020?
choices: It repealed its policy that players must stand for the anthem.
It banned the anthem at all matches.
It moved the women's team to a new federation.
It adopted a new rule requiring players to kneel.
check.why: U.S. Soccer adopted a stand-for-the-anthem policy in 2017 and voted to repeal it in June 2020.

check.q: What is a federation in sport?
choices: a national or world body that governs a sport
a city that owns a stadium
check.why: A federation, like U.S. Soccer, governs a sport and its national teams.

lessons.title: Kneeling in 2016
lessons.mainIdea: In 2016 NFL quarterback Colin Kaepernick sat, then knelt, during the anthem to protest police violence and racial injustice, and the protest spread across sports.
reading: In August 2016, San Francisco 49ers quarterback Colin Kaepernick sat on the bench during the anthem at preseason games. Asked why, he said he was protesting the treatment of Black people and police violence. He then spoke with Nate Boyer, a former Army Green Beret and former NFL player. After that talk, Kaepernick began kneeling instead of sitting.

Teammate Eric Reid knelt beside him. Other players across the NFL knelt, sat or raised fists during the season. Some high school and college athletes did the same. Critics said kneeling disrespected the flag and the military. Supporters said kneeling was a quiet, respectful way to make a point during a national ritual.

Kaepernick opted out of his contract after the 2016 season and became a *free agent*, a player able to sign with any team. No team signed him. In 2017 he filed a *grievance* under the players' contract with the league, claiming the owners had worked together to keep him out. The grievance was settled in February 2019. The terms were kept private.

In May 2018 NFL owners approved a policy that players on the field must stand, but could stay in the locker room. The players' union objected, and the league soon put the policy on hold. In June 2020, commissioner Roger Goodell said the league had been wrong not to listen to players earlier. The history shows one protest moving through a contract, a union and an owners' vote.

words.d: a player whose contract has ended and who may sign with any team
a formal complaint filed under a union contract, decided by a set process
an organization that bargains with a league on behalf of its players

look.title: One Protest, Three Paths
look.text: A quarterback kneels during the anthem in 2016. The next year he is unsigned and files a grievance under the union contract. In 2018 team owners vote on an anthem policy. The union objects, and the policy is put on hold.
look.prompt: Which steps in this story happened on the field, and which happened in meeting rooms? Why do both matter?

check.q: Who did Colin Kaepernick speak with before he switched from sitting to kneeling?
check.why: He spoke with Nate Boyer, a former Green Beret and NFL player, and then began kneeling.

check.q: What is a grievance in a players' contract?
choices: a type of penalty on the field
a formal complaint decided by a set process
a new team's first-round draft pick
check.why: A grievance is a formal complaint filed under a union contract, as Kaepernick did in 2017.

check.q: What happened to the NFL's May 2018 anthem policy?
choices: It was written into federal law.
It was adopted by the NBA the next day.
It led to a Supreme Court case.
It was put on hold after the players' union objected.
check.why: The union objected, and the league put the 2018 policy on hold.

lessons.title: What the First Amendment Covers
lessons.mainIdea: The First Amendment limits what government may do about speech; a private league acts as an employer, so its rules come from contracts rather than the Constitution.
reading: The *First Amendment* was ratified in 1791 as part of the Bill of Rights. It protects freedom of speech, religion, the press and assembly. Its first words are "Congress shall make no law." Courts have read it to limit every level of government, including states, cities and public schools. It does not, by itself, limit private companies.

The NFL, the NBA and their teams are private businesses. A player there is an employee under a contract. What a player may do during the anthem is set by the league's rules and the *collective bargaining agreement*, the contract the union signs with the league. A private employer can make some rules about conduct at work that a government could not.

Yet many stadiums are not purely private. Soldier Field in Chicago is owned by the Chicago Park District, a public body. Many arenas were built or rebuilt with tax money. Anthems are national symbols, and flyovers often use military planes. These facts give the field some features of a *public square*, a shared place where citizens speak and argue.

Writers who study protest in sport often choose one frame and keep it. A labor frame asks what the contract allows. A legal frame asks whether a government actor is involved. A civic frame asks what a national ritual means in a shared space. Mixing frames without saying so leads to answers that seem to disagree but are really about different questions.

words.d: the part of the U.S. Constitution, ratified in 1791, that protects speech, religion, press and assembly from government
the contract a players' union and a league sign about pay, rules and discipline
a shared place where citizens gather to speak, argue and be seen
the lens a historian uses to ask questions, such as labor, law or civic life

look.title: The First Amendment
look.text: Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof; or abridging the freedom of speech, or of the press; or the right of the people peaceably to assemble, and to petition the Government for a redress of grievances.
look.cite: Constitution of the United States, First Amendment, ratified 1791
look.prompt: Which word in the first line shows who the amendment limits? What does that mean for a private sports league?

check.q: Whom does the First Amendment limit?
check.why: The amendment begins "Congress shall make no law," and courts apply it to all levels of government, not private companies.

check.q: What is a collective bargaining agreement?
choices: a law passed by Congress about sports
the contract a players' union and a league sign
check.why: It is the contract between the union and the league that sets pay, rules and discipline.

check.q: Who owns Soldier Field in Chicago?
check.why: Soldier Field is owned by the Chicago Park District, a public body.

lessons.title: Students at the Schoolhouse Gate
lessons.mainIdea: In Barnette (1943) and Tinker (1969), the Supreme Court ruled that public school students keep their rights to speech, including the right not to be forced to salute the flag.
reading: In the early 1940s, West Virginia required public school students to salute the flag and recite the Pledge of Allegiance. Children from Jehovah's Witness families refused. Their faith taught them not to salute images. Some were expelled. In 1943, in *West Virginia State Board of Education v. Barnette*, the Supreme Court ruled 6 to 3 that schools could not force the salute.

In December 1965, students in Des Moines, Iowa, wore black armbands to school to mourn the dead in the Vietnam War. They included John Tinker, 15, his sister Mary Beth Tinker, 13, and their friend Christopher Eckhardt, 16. The school had banned armbands just before. The students were sent home. Their families sued.

In 1969, in *Tinker v. Des Moines*, the Court ruled 7 to 2 for the students. Justice Abe Fortas wrote the opinion. The Court said a school may limit speech that would cause a *substantial disruption* of school work. A silent armband, the Court found, did not. That test still guides public schools today.

These cases matter for school sport because a public school is part of government. A student athlete on a public school team keeps these protections, though schools can still set rules to keep order. A private club or professional league is different, because it is not government. The same act can be judged by different rules in different places.

words.d: the 1943 Supreme Court case ruling that public schools may not force students to salute the flag
the 1969 Supreme Court case protecting students' silent protest at school
the Tinker test: a school may limit speech that would seriously interfere with school work

look.title: The Schoolhouse Gate
look.text: It can hardly be argued that either students or teachers shed their constitutional rights to freedom of speech or expression at the schoolhouse gate.
look.cite: Justice Abe Fortas, opinion of the Court, Tinker v. Des Moines Independent Community School District, 393 U.S. 503 (1969)
look.prompt: What does the schoolhouse gate stand for in this sentence? How might it apply to a public school's field or gym?

check.q: What did the Court decide in Barnette in 1943?
choices: Schools must play the anthem before games.
Public schools may not force students to salute the flag.
Private leagues must follow the First Amendment.
check.why: Barnette ruled 6 to 3 that public schools could not force a flag salute.

check.q: What did the Des Moines students wear in 1965?
check.why: The students wore black armbands to mourn those killed in the Vietnam War.

check.q: Why do Tinker and Barnette apply to public school teams but not to the NFL?
choices: A public school is part of government; the NFL is a private business.
The NFL is older than public schools.
The cases were only about football.
The NFL wrote the First Amendment.
check.why: The First Amendment limits government, which includes public schools but not private leagues.

lessons.title: A Coach at the Fifty-Yard Line
lessons.mainIdea: In Kennedy v. Bremerton School District (2022), the Supreme Court ruled 6 to 3 that a public school coach could pray alone at midfield after games.
reading: Joseph Kennedy was an assistant football coach at Bremerton High School in Washington State. For years he knelt at the fifty-yard line after games and prayed. Over time, players and others sometimes joined him. In 2015 the Bremerton School District asked him to stop praying on the field in ways that could look like the school backing a religion.

The district pointed to the *Establishment Clause*, the part of the First Amendment that bars government from setting up or favoring a religion. A coach is a public employee. The district worried that students might feel pressure to join. Kennedy kept praying after games. The district placed him on leave, and he did not reapply for the job.

Kennedy sued. The case reached the U.S. Supreme Court. On June 27, 2022, the Court ruled 6 to 3 in *Kennedy v. Bremerton School District*. Justice Neil Gorsuch wrote that the brief, quiet prayer was the coach's private religious exercise and speech, protected by the First Amendment. Justice Sonia Sotomayor wrote the dissent.

The dissent argued that a coach at midfield, right after a game, is still acting as a school official with power over players. The case shows the workplace and public-square frames colliding. The field is a school workplace. It is also a place where a person's own faith and speech are protected. Courts must decide which side weighs more.

words.d: the part of the First Amendment that bars government from setting up or favoring a religion
a person who works for a government body, such as a public school
a written opinion by judges who disagree with the Court's decision

lessons.title: The 1968 Boycott Call
lessons.mainIdea: In 1967 the Olympic Project for Human Rights called for Black athletes to boycott the 1968 Olympics; most competed, but some, like Lew Alcindor, stayed away.
reading: A *boycott* is a refusal to take part, used to press for change. In November 1967, Harry Edwards and a group of Black athletes met in Los Angeles. They proposed that Black athletes boycott the 1968 Olympic Games in Mexico City. The group became known as the Olympic Project for Human Rights.

The group listed demands. They asked that Muhammad Ali's heavyweight title be restored. They asked that Avery Brundage be removed as IOC president. They asked that South Africa and Rhodesia, both ruled by white minority governments, be kept out of the Games. Some athletes also backed a boycott of the New York Athletic Club, which barred Black and Jewish members.

The full Olympic boycott did not happen. Most Black athletes chose to compete and made their own decisions about how to protest. Some did not go. Lew Alcindor, the star center at UCLA, declined to try out for the 1968 basketball team. He later took the name *Kareem Abdul-Jabbar*. The U.S. team won the gold medal without him.

The IOC had invited South Africa back for 1968 in early 1968. Many African nations, and others, said they would stay away. The IOC then reversed the invitation. South Africa did not compete in 1968. That outcome showed that the threat of a boycott, even when not carried out in full, could change a decision by a sports body.

words.d: a refusal to take part in something, used to press for change
the basketball player, first named Lew Alcindor, who declined to try out for the 1968 Olympic team
a clear request that a protest group says must be met

lessons.title: Missouri Football, 2015
lessons.mainIdea: In November 2015, Black football players at the University of Missouri said they would not play until the university system's president resigned, and he resigned within days.
reading: In fall 2015, students at the University of Missouri in Columbia protested racist incidents on campus. A student group called itself Concerned Student 1950. The year 1950 marked when the university first admitted Black students. Graduate student Jonathan Butler began a hunger strike on November 2. He said he would not eat until University of Missouri System president Tim Wolfe left office.

On November 7, Black players on the Missouri football team announced they would not practice or play until Wolfe resigned. Head coach Gary Pinkel and many teammates backed them. The next game was against Brigham Young University. News reports said the school could owe BYU about one million dollars if it did not play.

Tim Wolfe resigned on November 9, 2015. The campus chancellor stepped down the same day. The team returned to practice and played the BYU game that week. The case drew national attention because college players are not employees and have no union. Even so, their refusal to play had real power over the university.

The Missouri protest showed where power sits in college sport. A *revenue sport* like football brings in money from tickets, television and contracts. When players in that sport refuse to take the field, the school's budget and schedule are at stake. That gives them leverage, a kind of bargaining power, even without a formal contract.

bargaining power that comes from what the other side stands to lose

lessons.title: The Bucks Stay Inside, 2020
lessons.mainIdea: On August 26, 2020, the Milwaukee Bucks refused to take the floor for a playoff game after police shot Jacob Blake in Kenosha, Wisconsin, and other leagues paused too.
reading: In 2020 the COVID-19 pandemic stopped most sports in March. The NBA restarted in July inside a closed site at Walt Disney World near Orlando, Florida. Players, coaches and staff lived and played there without fans. People called it the *bubble*. The league and the players' union agreed that players could wear approved social justice messages on their jerseys.

On August 23, 2020, a police officer in Kenosha, Wisconsin, shot Jacob Blake, a Black man, several times in the back. Blake survived but was left paralyzed from the waist down. Kenosha is about forty miles south of Milwaukee. Three days later, the Milwaukee Bucks were set to play the Orlando Magic in Game 5 of a first-round playoff series.

The Bucks stayed in their locker room and did not come out for the game. It was a *wildcat strike*, a work stoppage started by workers without the formal approval of their union. The NBA postponed that day's playoff games. The WNBA postponed its games. Some Major League Baseball, Major League Soccer and tennis events were also postponed.

The players met and voted on what to do next. Play resumed on August 29. As part of the agreement, many NBA teams that owned their arenas offered them as voting sites for the 2020 election. The strike showed that players, not only owners, could stop the schedule. It happened inside a league-run workplace that was also a national stage.

words.d: the closed site near Orlando where the NBA finished its 2020 season during the pandemic
a work stoppage started by workers without formal union approval
to move an event to a later time

chapters.title: Two Tours, Not One Ladder
chapters.bigQuestion: Are women's and men's professional sports two rungs on one ladder, or two separate industries with their own histories, money and media?

story.title: Two Calendars on a Wall
story.kicker: Two tour schedules hang side by side, and the prize lines do not match.
paragraphs: A sports reporter pins two printed calendars on the wall above her desk. One lists the season of a men's professional tennis tour. The other lists the season of a women's tour. Many of the same cities appear on both. Some weeks, both tours play at the same event, on courts a few steps apart.

Next to each tournament, the calendars list prize money. At the four biggest tournaments, the numbers for men and women match. At many other weeks, they do not. The men's line is often higher. The reporter circles the gaps with a red pen and writes the dollar amounts in the margin.

She knows the two tours are separate businesses. Each has its own rulebook, its own ranking list, its own sponsors and its own television deals. Each was founded by players in the early 1970s. Women players had to fight just to get their own tournaments at all. That history shapes every number on the page.

Her editor asks a simple question: are the women behind the men, or on a different road? The answer depends on history. It depends on who built each tour, when, and with whose money. It also depends on who has held the cameras over the past hundred years.
story.think: Why might it matter whether we describe women's sport as a lower rung of men's sport or as its own industry?

lessons.title: A Wartime League in Rockford
lessons.mainIdea: Chicago Cubs owner Philip K. Wrigley started the All-American Girls Professional Baseball League in 1943; it ran in Midwestern cities until 1954.
reading: Women played baseball long before any women's league was paid. College women at Vassar formed teams in the 1860s. Traveling "Bloomer Girls" teams played men's town teams from the 1890s into the 1930s. They earned money from gate receipts, the ticket sales at each game. Those teams were barnstorming clubs, not a league with a fixed schedule.

In 1943, during World War II, many major league players were in the military. Philip K. Wrigley, owner of the Chicago Cubs and the Wrigley chewing gum company, feared ballparks might close. He founded what became the *All-American Girls Professional Baseball League* (AAGPBL). Its first four teams were the Rockford Peaches, the Racine Belles, the Kenosha Comets and the South Bend Blue Sox.

The league grew to ten teams at its peak, all in Midwestern cities. More than 600 women played in it over twelve seasons. Players had to follow rules about dress and conduct off the field. The league was also *segregated*: it did not sign Black players. A few Black women, such as Toni Stone, played instead in the Negro Leagues in the 1950s.

The AAGPBL folded after the 1954 season. Television, falling attendance and the return of men's baseball all hurt it. The Rockford Peaches played in Rockford, Illinois, for the league's whole run. The 1992 film A League of Their Own brought new attention to the league, and the Baseball Hall of Fame opened an exhibit on it in 1988.

words.d: the women's pro league founded by Philip K. Wrigley in 1943 that ran until 1954

lessons.title: Thirteen Golfers Found a Tour
lessons.mainIdea: In 1950 thirteen women golfers, including Babe Didrikson Zaharias and Patty Berg, founded the Ladies Professional Golf Association.
reading: Golf clubs in the United States and Britain were often private. Many limited women to certain days or hours. Women still built their own events. The U.S. Women's Amateur began in 1895, the same year as the men's U.S. Amateur. But in the 1940s there were few paid events for women professionals.

In 1950 thirteen women founded the *Ladies Professional Golf Association*, or LPGA. The founders included Babe Didrikson Zaharias, Patty Berg and Louise Suggs. Patty Berg served as its first president. The players ran the tour themselves in the early years. They planned events, handled entries and helped find sponsors.

Zaharias was already famous. At the 1932 Olympics in Los Angeles, she won gold in the javelin and the 80-meter hurdles and silver in the high jump. She then became the best-known woman golfer of her time. She won the U.S. Women's Open in 1948, 1950 and 1954. The 1954 win came after cancer surgery the year before.

The LPGA is often called the oldest continuing women's professional sports organization in the United States. Men's golf followed a different path. The PGA of America was founded in 1916 for club *professionals*. In 1968 touring pros broke away and formed what became the PGA Tour. The two golf tours grew side by side, each with its own rules and money.

words.d: the Ladies Professional Golf Association, founded in 1950 by thirteen women golfers
a person paid to play or teach a sport
a season of events in one sport run by one organization, traveling from place to place

lessons.title: Nine Players, One Dollar
lessons.mainIdea: In 1970 nine women tennis players signed one-dollar contracts with Gladys Heldman to play a Houston event, starting the tour that led to the WTA.
reading: Tennis turned *open* in 1968. That meant professionals and amateurs could play in the same tournaments, including Wimbledon. Prize money grew fast, but mostly for men. At the 1970 Pacific Southwest Championships in Los Angeles, the men's winner was offered $12,500. The women's winner was offered $1,500.

Billie Jean King and other women players protested the gap. Gladys Heldman, publisher of World Tennis magazine, set up a separate women's event in Houston in September 1970. The U.S. Lawn Tennis Association, which governed the sport, would not approve it. Players who entered risked suspension from official events.

Nine women signed contracts for one dollar each with Heldman to become professionals. They are remembered as the *Original 9*. They included Billie Jean King, Rosie Casals, Nancy Richey, Kerry Melville and Julie Heldman. The cigarette brand Virginia Slims sponsored the Houston event. Rosie Casals won it.

From that single event grew the Virginia Slims Circuit, a full tour for women in 1971. King became the first woman athlete to earn more than $100,000 in prize money in a single year, in 1971. The tour gave women their own schedule and their own sponsor. It also showed that a women's event could sell tickets without being attached to a men's one.

words.d: the system, starting in 1968, that let professionals and amateurs play in the same tournaments
the nine women who signed one-dollar contracts in 1970 to start a women's pro tour

lessons.title: A Union at a London Hotel
lessons.mainIdea: Men players formed the ATP in 1972 and women players formed the WTA in 1973, creating two separate player-run tours.
reading: In 1972 men players formed the *Association of Tennis Professionals*, or ATP, at the U.S. Open. It began as a players' group to protect their interests. In 1973 the ATP showed its strength. Most of its members boycotted Wimbledon after the Yugoslav federation suspended Niki Pilić and the world governing body backed the ban.

Women players met at the Gloucester Hotel in London in June 1973, the week before Wimbledon. Billie Jean King led the meeting. More than sixty players agreed to form the *Women's Tennis Association*, or WTA. King was its first president. The group gave women one voice when they bargained with tournaments and sponsors.

That same year, the U.S. Open became the first of the four biggest tournaments, the *Grand Slams*, to pay men and women equal prize money. King had pressed for it. A deodorant company added money to close the gap. It would take the other three Grand Slam events decades to follow.

Today the ATP runs the men's tour and the WTA runs the women's tour. They keep separate rankings and separate calendars. The four Grand Slams are run by national federations, not by either tour. Some events, such as the tournament at Indian Wells, California, hold men's and women's draws in the same week.

the Women's Tennis Association, formed in London in 1973 with Billie Jean King as first president
one of tennis's four biggest tournaments: the Australian Open, French Open, Wimbledon and U.S. Open

lessons.title: The Match in the Astrodome
lessons.mainIdea: On September 20, 1973, Billie Jean King beat Bobby Riggs in the Houston Astrodome in a televised match called the Battle of the Sexes.
reading: Bobby Riggs had won Wimbledon in 1939. By 1973 he was 55 years old and a well-known promoter of himself. He claimed that even an older man could beat the best women players. In May 1973 he beat Margaret Court of Australia, then the top-ranked woman, in a televised match. Newspapers called it the Mother's Day Massacre.

Billie Jean King accepted his challenge for a match in the Houston *Astrodome*, a domed stadium. It was set for September 20, 1973. The prize was $100,000, winner take all. ABC television carried it in prime time. The crowd of more than 30,000 was one of the largest ever to watch a tennis match at that time.

King won in straight sets, 6–4, 6–3, 6–3. The match was a *spectacle*, a show built for a crowd and cameras. It came one year after Title IX and a few months after the WTA was founded. King said later that she felt she had to win to protect the new women's tour and the push for equal pay.

Historians see the match as a media event more than a sports test. It pitted a 29-year-old champion against a 55-year-old retired player. Still, the audience was huge, and the result was used in arguments about women's place in sport. The match showed how television could turn a question about money into a national show.

words.d: the 1973 televised match in which Billie Jean King beat Bobby Riggs
the domed stadium in Houston, Texas, opened in 1965
an event staged as a show for a large crowd or audience

lessons.title: The WNBA Tips Off
lessons.mainIdea: The NBA founded the WNBA in 1996; it began play in 1997 and outlasted a rival women's league, the ABL.
reading: Women's professional basketball had tried before. The Women's Professional Basketball League played from 1978 to 1981 and then folded. Money and small crowds hurt it. College women's basketball grew after Title IX in 1972. The NCAA held its first women's tournament in 1982. Before that, the Association for Intercollegiate Athletics for Women ran women's college championships.

The 1996 U.S. Olympic women's team won gold in Atlanta. Its success drew crowds. That same year two new women's leagues formed. The American Basketball League (ABL) began play in the fall of 1996. The NBA's board of governors approved the *Women's National Basketball Association*, or WNBA, in April 1996.

The WNBA played its first game on June 21, 1997. It had eight teams, owned by the NBA and paired with NBA cities. It played in summer, when NBA arenas were free. The ABL paid many players more but had less money behind it. The ABL stopped play in December 1998, and many of its players joined the WNBA.

The WNBA began as a *single-entity* league, with the NBA owning all teams. Over time, teams were sold to separate owners. The Chicago Sky joined as an expansion team in 2006 and won the league title in 2021. The league's history shows a women's league built inside a men's league's business, then slowly standing on its own.

a league in which one owner, not separate owners, controls all teams
a new team added to an existing league

lessons.title: Equal Pay, Slam by Slam
lessons.mainIdea: The four Grand Slams reached equal prize money at different times, from the U.S. Open in 1973 to Wimbledon in 2007.
reading: Each Grand Slam tournament is run by a different national body. The U.S. Open is run by the United States Tennis Association. Wimbledon is run by the All England Lawn Tennis and Croquet Club. The French Open is run by the French Tennis Federation. The Australian Open is run by Tennis Australia. Each decided on *equal prize money* on its own schedule.

The U.S. Open paid equally in 1973. The Australian Open paid equally in 2001. The French Open paid the two singles champions equally in 2006 and made all prize money equal in 2007. Wimbledon, the oldest of the four, held out longest. It had first held a women's singles event in 1884, seven years after the first men's event in 1877.

In 2006 Venus Williams wrote an essay in The Times of London. She argued that Wimbledon's unequal pay sent women a message that they were second class. The WTA and players had pressed the club for years. In February 2007 Wimbledon announced it would pay equally. Venus Williams won the women's title that summer.

Critics of equal pay pointed out that men played best-of-five sets at Grand Slams and women played best-of-three. Supporters answered that prize money follows tickets, television and the value of the event, not minutes on court. The argument is a real one about how an industry sets pay. The history shows each club made its own choice.

lessons.title: World Cup Prize Pools
lessons.mainIdea: FIFA sets separate prize pools for the men's and women's World Cups, and in 2018–2019 the men's pool was more than thirteen times the women's.
reading: FIFA, founded in 1904, runs the men's World Cup, first held in Uruguay in 1930. The first FIFA Women's World Cup came much later, in China in 1991. Women's soccer had been popular in England around 1920. Then, in 1921, England's Football Association banned women from playing on its members' grounds. That ban lasted until 1971.

Each World Cup has a *prize pool*, the total money FIFA pays to the teams. FIFA pays the pool to national federations, which decide what share goes to players. The men's World Cup brings in far more from television and sponsors. FIFA has set each pool based partly on that income.

For the 2018 men's World Cup in Russia, the prize pool was 400 million dollars. For the 2019 Women's World Cup in France, it was 30 million dollars. For 2022 in Qatar, the men's pool was 440 million dollars. For 2023 in Australia and New Zealand, FIFA raised the women's pool to 110 million dollars.

Naming the gap in dollars helps separate two questions. One question is how much money each event brings in. Another is how much of that money goes to players. Women's teams argued that FIFA and national federations had invested less in women's soccer for decades, so lower income partly reflected lower investment.

words.d: the world governing body for soccer, founded in 1904
the total money an organizer pays to teams or players at an event
money spent now to build something that may earn more later

lessons.title: A Lawsuit and a Contract
lessons.mainIdea: The U.S. women's national soccer team sued U.S. Soccer in 2019, and in 2022 the two sides signed contracts giving men's and women's teams equal pay.
reading: The U.S. women's national team won the Women's World Cup in 1991, 1999, 2015 and 2019. The men's national team has never won it. In 2016, five women players filed a complaint with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, a federal agency. They said U.S. Soccer paid them less than the men for the same work.

On March 8, 2019, International Women's Day, 28 players sued U.S. Soccer in federal court. The lead name on the case was Alex Morgan. They sued under the *Equal Pay Act* of 1963 and Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. The Equal Pay Act bars employers from paying women less than men for equal work in the same workplace.

In 2020 a federal judge ruled against the players on the pay claim. The players appealed. In February 2022 the two sides settled. U.S. Soccer agreed to pay 24 million dollars. Most of it went to the players as back pay, and part went to a fund for players' charities and careers after soccer.

In May 2022 U.S. Soccer signed new *collective bargaining agreements* with both the men's and women's players' unions. The contracts set equal pay for national team games. They also pooled World Cup prize money from FIFA and split it between both teams. U.S. Soccer said it was the first federation in the world to do this.

words.d: a 1963 U.S. law that bars paying women less than men for equal work
an agreement that ends a lawsuit without a final court ruling
money owed for past work that was paid too little

lessons.title: A Law That Filled Rosters
lessons.mainIdea: Title IX of 1972 barred sex discrimination in federally funded schools, and girls' high school sports grew from about 295,000 players to millions.
reading: *Title IX* is part of the Education Amendments of 1972. President Richard Nixon signed it on June 23, 1972. It is only 37 words long in its main sentence. It says no person may be shut out of any education program that gets federal money because of sex. It does not name sport, but schools soon learned it covered athletics.

Before Title IX, girls' school sports were small. The National Federation of State High School Associations counts players every year. In the 1971–72 school year it counted about 295,000 girls in high school sports. By the 2018–19 school year the count was more than 3.4 million. Boys' numbers also grew in those years.

Illinois had its own history. The IHSA, founded in 1900, added girls' state championships in many sports during the 1970s. Before that, many girls played only in play days or intramural games. Those were events inside one school or among a few schools, without state titles. The new state series gave girls a *pipeline* to college teams.

Title IX built the pipeline that later fed pro leagues and national teams. Many members of the 1996 Olympic basketball and 1999 World Cup soccer teams grew up after 1972. Historians often note that the law changed schools first and professional sport only later. That order helps explain why women's pro leagues grew most after the 1990s.

lessons.title: Crowds in 1999, Cameras Since
lessons.mainIdea: The 1999 Women's World Cup final drew 90,185 fans to the Rose Bowl, yet long-running studies found women's sports got a small share of TV sports news.
reading: On July 10, 1999, the United States played China in the Women's World Cup final at the Rose Bowl in Pasadena, California. The crowd was 90,185, then a record for a women's sports event. The game ended 0–0 and was decided by penalty kicks. The United States won. The final drew a large U.S. television audience.

Big crowds did not change daily sports news right away. In 1989 sociologist Michael Messner and colleagues began studying *airtime*, the minutes TV news gives each story, on Los Angeles stations. Later rounds were led with Cheryl Cooky. Across three decades, their studies found women's sports got well under one tenth of sports news airtime.

Media difference also meant different kinds of coverage. The studies found that women athletes were more often shown in ways not tied to their sport. Coverage of men's sport was more likely to include highlights, music and excited talk. Researchers call the amount and style of coverage *visibility*. Less visibility can mean fewer fans, and fewer fans can mean less money.

Television deals are a central part of sports income. A league with more airtime can sell more ads and higher-priced rights. The media gap and the money gap are linked. Historians describe a cycle: little investment and coverage led to smaller audiences, which were then used to justify little investment and coverage.

words.d: the minutes a TV or radio program gives to a story
how often and how fully a team or sport is seen in media
the right, sold by a league, to broadcast its games

lessons.title: Two Weight Rooms, 2021
lessons.mainIdea: In 2021 photos of an unequal weight room at the NCAA women's basketball tournament led to an outside review and a shared March Madness name.
reading: The NCAA men's basketball tournament began in 1939. The NCAA women's tournament began in 1982. For years the NCAA used the brand *March Madness* only for the men. In 2021, because of the pandemic, the NCAA held each tournament in one area: the men near Indianapolis and the women in and around San Antonio, Texas.

In March 2021, players and staff posted photos online. The men's weight room had rows of full equipment. The women's space had one rack of small dumbbells. Oregon forward Sedona Prince posted a widely shared video. Players also noted differences in food, gifts and COVID-19 testing. The NCAA added a full weight room for the women within days.

The NCAA then hired the law firm Kaplan Hecker & Fink for an outside *gender equity* review. Its report, released in August 2021, found that the NCAA's structure put men's basketball first. It found that the NCAA's television deal bundled the women's tournament with other championships. That arrangement, the report said, undervalued the women's event.

In 2022 the NCAA began using the March Madness name for the women's tournament too. Audiences grew. In April 2024, the women's championship game between South Carolina and Iowa drew about 19 million viewers on average. That was more than the men's final that year, about 15 million. Iowa's Caitlin Clark had become the all-time leading scorer in NCAA Division I basketball that season.

words.d: the NCAA's brand for its basketball tournaments, used for the women's tournament since 2022

a study done by people not employed by the organization being studied
